<!-- Generated by `khora doc` from the `///` and `//!` comments in `std::crypto`. Edits here are overwritten; change the source. -->

Digests, message authentication, constant-time comparison, hex and base64,
and random bytes from the operating system.

**Bound, not written.** SHA-2, HMAC and the random source are `ring`'s,
the library rustls is built on and every Khora executable already links. A
digest written out by hand produces output that looks exactly like a
digest when it is wrong, and no test of its own tells the difference.

Signing and checking a webhook is the case this module is shaped around:

```khora
let key = Redacted::of(String::bytes(secret));
let header = "sha256=${Hex::encode(Hmac::sha256(key, String::bytes(body)))}";
// and on receipt, never with `==`:
let genuine = match Hex::decode(received) {
  Option::Some(tag) => Hmac::verify_sha256(key, String::bytes(body), tag),
  Option::None => false,
};
```

**Keys are `Redacted`.** Every function that takes a key takes a
`Redacted<Array<U8>>`, so a key shows as `<redacted>` in a log line or an
interpolation, a record holding one cannot derive `Encode`, and nothing here
hands the bytes back. The only way to them is `Redacted::expose`, written
where somebody can search for it.

## What is not here, and why

No ciphers, no authenticated encryption, no signatures (Ed25519, ECDSA), no
key exchange and no password hashing. Each is a choice of algorithm,
parameters and nonce rules that has to stay correct for as long as data
encrypted or signed with it exists, and each has failure modes, a reused
nonce or a weak work factor, that no type in this module can prevent. A
hash and a MAC have no such parameters: SHA-256 is SHA-256. TLS, which is
where most programs need encryption, is in `std::net::tls`. For password
storage, use a dedicated argon2 or scrypt library through the foreign
function interface; a fast hash such as SHA-256 is the wrong tool there,
because being fast is what makes guessing passwords cheap.

Not available when compiling for WebAssembly, which has no operating
system random source and no build of `ring`.

## Types

### Hmac

```khora
pub type Hmac;
```

Message authentication with a shared key (RFC 2104).

A namespace for four functions: sign with `sha256` or `sha512`, and check a
tag you were sent with `verify_sha256` or `verify_sha512`. **Check with
`verify`, never by comparing tags with `==`.** `==` stops at the first byte
that differs, so how long it takes tells a caller how much of a forged tag
was right, and a forger who can time it learns the real tag a byte at a
time.

### Hex

```khora
pub type Hex;
```

Bytes as hexadecimal text, two digits a byte.

### Base64

```khora
pub type Base64;
```

Bytes as base64 text (RFC 4648).

Two alphabets. `encode` and `decode` are the standard one, `+` and `/`
with `=` padding, which is what MIME, HTTP Basic authentication and most
APIs mean by "base64". The `url_safe` pair is RFC 4648 §5, `-` and `_`
**without padding**, which is what JWTs, URL parameters and cookie values
use, because `+`, `/` and `=` all need escaping there.

**Decoding is strict.** Characters outside the alphabet, whitespace and
line breaks included, are refused; so is missing or misplaced padding in
the standard variant, any padding in the URL-safe one, and unused bits that
are not zero. Each value then has exactly one encoding, so a signature
compared after decoding cannot be altered in transit and still match.

## Effects

### SecureRandom

```khora
pub effect SecureRandom {
  bytes: (Array<U8>) -> (),
}
```

Random bytes nobody can predict: for keys, tokens, session identifiers and
nonces.

**Not `std::random::Random`.** That one is a fast generator anybody can
predict from a single draw, which is what a shuffle or a test wants and
exactly wrong for a secret. Two capabilities with two names, so a signature
says which one a function needed.

A capability so that a test can supply the bytes. There is deliberately no
way to seed the real one: a test that wants fixed bytes writes a handler
that fills the buffer with them.

```khora
fn new_token() -> String with { random: SecureRandom } {
  let bytes: Array<U8> = Array::new(32, U8::of(0));
  random.bytes(bytes);
  Base64::encode_url_safe(bytes)
}
```

Drawing needs no grant in the manifest. A grant limits what a program can
reach, a file or a host or another program, and reading random bytes
reaches nothing a dependency could misuse; the capability in the
signature already says it happens.

#### bytes

```khora
bytes: (Array<U8>) ->()
```

Fills every element of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.

## Methods

### Hmac

```khora
impl Hmac
```

#### sha256

```khora
pub fn sha256(key: Redacted<Array<U8>>, message: Array<U8>) -> Array<U8>
```

The HMAC-SHA-256 tag of `message` under `key`: 32 bytes.

A key of any length is accepted. RFC 2104 recommends at least the
digest's width, 32 bytes; [`SecureRandom`](#securerandom) is where one comes from.

#### sha512

```khora
pub fn sha512(key: Redacted<Array<U8>>, message: Array<U8>) -> Array<U8>
```

The HMAC-SHA-512 tag of `message` under `key`: 64 bytes.

#### verify_sha256

```khora
pub fn verify_sha256(key: Redacted<Array<U8>>, message: Array<U8>, tag: Array<U8>) -> Bool
```

Whether `tag` is the HMAC-SHA-256 of `message` under `key`.

**The comparison takes the same time wherever the tags differ**, so a
forger learns nothing from timing it. A tag of the wrong length,
including an empty or truncated one, is `false`: accepting a prefix of
the tag would let a forger guess a few bytes instead of thirty-two.

#### verify_sha512

```khora
pub fn verify_sha512(key: Redacted<Array<U8>>, message: Array<U8>, tag: Array<U8>) -> Bool
```

Whether `tag` is the HMAC-SHA-512 of `message` under `key`, in constant
time, as [`Hmac::verify_sha256`](#verify_sha256).


`bytes` as lowercase hex: `[255, 1]` is `ff01`.

#### decode

```khora
pub fn decode(text: String) -> Option<Array<U8>>
```

The bytes `text` spells, or `None` if it is not hex.

Either case is accepted. An odd number of digits, whitespace, a `0x`
prefix or any other character is `None`.

### SecureRandom

```khora
impl SecureRandom
```

#### real

```khora
pub fn real() -> SecureRandom
```

The operating system's generator: `getrandom` on Linux, `getentropy` on
macOS, `ProcessPrng` on Windows.

If the operating system cannot supply random bytes, the program stops
rather than continuing with weaker ones: a key made from anything else is
a key an attacker can make too.

## Functions

### sha256

```khora
pub fn sha256(bytes: Array<U8>) -> Array<U8>
```

The SHA-256 digest of `bytes`: 32 bytes.

For a checksum, a content address or a cache key. **Not for a password**:
see the module's note on what is not here. To sign something, use
`Hmac::sha256`; a digest of a secret followed by a message can be
extended by anyone who sees it.

```khora
Hex::encode(sha256(String::bytes("abc")))
// ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad
```

### sha512

```khora
pub fn sha512(bytes: Array<U8>) -> Array<U8>
```

The SHA-512 digest of `bytes`: 64 bytes.

### constant_time_eq

```khora
pub fn constant_time_eq(a: Array<U8>, b: Array<U8>) -> Bool
```

Whether `a` and `b` hold the same bytes, in time that does not depend on
where they first differ.

For comparing a secret value you were sent against the one you hold, such as
an API token or a session identifier, where `==` would leak through its
timing how much of a guess was right. To check an HMAC tag, use
[`Hmac::verify_sha256`](#verify_sha256), which computes the tag as well.

**Arrays of different lengths are `false` at once**, so the time does show
whether the lengths matched, though nothing about the contents. That is
harmless when the length is public, as it is for a fixed-width token or a
digest; compare digests of the two values if it is not.

### pbkdf2_sha256

```khora
pub fn pbkdf2_sha256(password: Redacted<Array<U8>>, salt: Array<U8>, iterations: Int) -> Option<Redacted<Array<U8>>>
```

PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 of `password` and `salt` over `iterations` rounds,
32 bytes, or `None` for a count of zero or one too large.

What SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication derives a key with, which is the reason it
is here. **Not a recommendation for storing passwords**: PBKDF2 can be
computed cheaply on a GPU, and new designs should use argon2 or scrypt.

The result is `Redacted` because it stands in for the password: in SCRAM,
whoever holds it can log in. Hand it straight to `Hmac::sha256` as a key.
